content.rendered:
NIGERIA’S proposed $5 billion Total Return Swap arrangement with First Abu Dhabi Bank is perhaps the most innovative sovereign financing transaction ever attempted by the country. It may also become one of the most consequential.

Therefore, the warnings issued by the International Monetary Fund and Fitch Ratings deserve careful consideration, not because they signal imminent disaster, but because they identify the exact vulnerabilities that have historically plunged developing economies into debt distress.

The IMF and Fitch are not arguing that the transaction is inherently reckless. Rather, they warn that its complexity, opacity and contingent liabilities require unusually strong risk management.

The deal has some similarities to the “crude-for-cash” deals executed by the NNPC under the Muhammadu Buhari administration, which carried significant risks of oil price volatility.

Nigeria would do well to listen.

Unlike conventional Eurobonds, a Total Return Swap allows a country to obtain foreign currency liquidity by pledging domestic bonds as collateral.

In this case, Nigeria reportedly intends to use naira-denominated government securities valued at roughly $6.7 billion (133 per cent of the loan amount) to secure approximately $5 billion in hard-currency financing from First Abu Dhabi Bank, with maturity expected around 2032.

In effect, the government obtains dollars without immediately issuing expensive Eurobonds in volatile international markets.

The facility is intended to refinance more costly domestic and external debts, while supporting budget implementation and priority infrastructure projects. Reports suggest that the Federal Government has already drawn about $1.5 billion from the $5 billion arrangement in recent weeks.

The deal diversifies funding sources, broadens investor participation, improves liquidity management and potentially lowers borrowing costs.

For a country still rebuilding investor confidence after years of foreign exchange shortages, this appears attractive.

But the advantages come with substantial risks. Both the IMF and Fitch highlight the same concerns.

The precise contractual terms, including pricing mechanisms, valuation thresholds, margin requirements, fees, termination clauses and collateral conditions, remain largely undisclosed. Such opacity weakens legislative oversight, limits market understanding, and creates uncertainty about the country’s true debt exposure.

Should domestic bond prices fall, interest rates rise sharply, or the naira weaken significantly, Nigeria may be required to post additional collateral or make cash payments in dollars. Such demands typically emerge during periods of economic stress, exactly when foreign exchange liquidity is already under pressure.

Angola’s experience highlights the risks of such deals. After securing a $1 billion total return swap from JPMorgan in December 2024, the country faced a $200 million margin call in April 2025 when falling oil prices and market volatility eroded the value of the sovereign bonds pledged as collateral. The money was, however, returned when market conditions recovered.

Fitch rightly notes that there is no established precedent for how TRSs would be treated in sovereign debt restructurings. Would such obligations rank ahead of bondholders? Would pledged collateral remain protected? Would conventional creditors suffer larger losses?

No one knows. That uncertainty alone justifies caution.

Yet there is another side to the argument. Nigeria today is not the Angola of yesterday.

The country enters this transaction with stronger external buffers than it possessed several years ago. Foreign exchange reserves have reportedly climbed above $51 billion, their highest level in nearly two decades.

The exchange rate has stabilised significantly, with the naira trading within a relatively narrow band of N15 to N40 at NFEM. The gap between official and parallel market rates has also narrowed considerably to below N40.

Indeed, the IMF itself recently noted that the naira may remain undervalued by approximately 25 per cent according to its assessment models.

That observation is important since a stronger underlying currency position reduces immediate exchange rate risks. Stable reserves provide additional protection against external shocks. Improved foreign portfolio inflows and higher autonomous inflows have strengthened the CBN’s capacity to defend the currency.

These factors partly explain why the government may feel comfortable pursuing a TRS financing structure.

The country’s debt profile also requires a proper perspective. While total debts have surged to N159 trillion, claims that the current administration has borrowed more externally than all previous democratic governments combined do not withstand scrutiny.

According to Think Business Africa, Nigeria’s external debt rose from about $42.5 billion when President Bola Tinubu took office in May 2023 to roughly $51.9 billion by the end of 2025, an increase of $9.4 billion. By comparison, external debt increased by $32.6 billion under the Buhari administration, rising from $10.3 billion in 2015 to about $42.9 billion in 2023.

The issue, therefore, is not simply the volume of borrowing but the quality, structure and productivity of debt.

Several borrowings under the current administration have come from multilateral institutions such as the World Bank and African Development Bank, often on concessional terms. Additional facilities target power, education, agriculture, digital infrastructure and social interventions.

Nonetheless, Nigeria’s fiscal position remains fragile.

Debt service continues to consume almost half of revenues. The revenue-to-GDP ratio, at 11.3 per cent, remains well below the African average of 16 per cent and the AU-recommended 15 per cent minimum.

Benchmark interest rates remain painfully high at 26.5 per cent. Inflation, at 15.93 per cent (May), still burdens households and businesses.

This makes fiscal discipline essential. The IMF’s recommendation of a broadly neutral fiscal stance deserves attention. Government spending must become more efficient. Budget implementation cannot continue with endless carryovers. Revenue mobilisation must improve. Tax administration should become stronger while protecting vulnerable populations.

The CBN must also gradually lower interest rates as inflation moderates.

Current borrowing costs (ranging between 20 per cent and over 46 per cent once fees, management charges, and risk premiums are factored in) are choking investment, suppressing credit expansion and slowing economic growth.

Lower rates would reduce debt-servicing costs, support private sector expansion, and help improve domestic bond valuations, thereby reducing some of the very risks associated with the swap arrangement.

Preserving investor confidence is equally important.

Nigeria’s recent foreign exchange stability depends heavily on sustained capital inflows. Any sudden loss of confidence could trigger capital flight, pressure reserves, and destabilise the naira. Transparent disclosure of the swap terms would therefore reassure investors, rating agencies and markets.

Yet economic fundamentals must ultimately carry the burden.

Higher oil and gas production remains indispensable. Recent investments provide some encouragement.

The Bonga North project, increased commitments by international oil companies, growing output from indigenous producers and expanded natural gas investments all offer opportunities for higher export earnings.

Non-oil exports must also expand substantially. Agriculture, manufacturing, solid minerals and services exports remain underdeveloped, accounting for less than 10 per cent of total exports combined, according to the International Trade Administration. Increased export diversification would provide more sustainable foreign exchange earnings than financial engineering.

Improved tax collection is equally important. Nigeria cannot continue financing development primarily through borrowing while maintaining a comparatively weak revenue performance.

Most importantly, every external borrowing must be for infrastructure, especially electricity supply, transportation, ports, railways, healthcare, education and industrial productivity that can generate future growth that pays for the debt.

Nigerians can tolerate borrowing when they see roads built, power supplied, businesses expanding, jobs created and living standards improving.

What they cannot accept is debt without development, while pain and suffering persist.

Still, the First Abu Dhabi Bank transaction may ultimately become a useful addition to Nigeria’s financing toolbox. It could open an alternative pathway to expensive Eurobond issuances and help diversify funding sources for African sovereigns.

But innovation cannot replace prudence. The IMF and Fitch have done Nigeria a favour by identifying the risks early.

Their warnings are not arguments against the transaction itself. They are arguments for transparency, stronger disclosure, prudent fiscal management and careful monitoring.

If they are ignored, the swap could become another hidden liability. If they are embraced, Nigeria may pioneer a new financing model that balances innovation with stability.

The difference will lie not in the instrument itself, but in the discipline with which it is managed.
